source.title: Scaling Laws of Graph Neural Networks for Atomistic Materials Modeling*
source.authors: Chao-Jian Li; Zhi-Fan Ye; Massimiliano Lupo Pasini; Jong Youl Choi; Cheng Wan; Y. Lin; Prasanna Balaprakash

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. Some figure and page-layout text is flattened, but the study and its reported findings are readable.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests scaling in atomistic-materials GNNs and reports diminishing returns with model size, in contrast to the near-linear log-parameter trend it attributes to language and image models. This challenges the transfer of the same scaling form to this setting.
record.gate_note: The study reports model-size and dataset-size sweeps and depth/width effects. The language- and image-model scaling results mentioned in the introduction are cited context, not results from this study. The memory-optimization results in Section V do not measure the claim's scaling behavior and are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: The study's own sweeps scale equivariant GNNs from 0.1M to 2B parameters and training data from 0.1 to 1.2 TB on atomistic energy/force prediction. It reports held-out test loss in each sweep. This is a new setting for V5 (a non-text modality). It fits no power law and makes no extrapolation or compute-optimal analysis.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that scaling both model and data lowers test loss. Model-size gains diminish, which they attribute to GNN locality versus Transformer attention, and current architectures may bottleneck beyond 2B parameters. Data scaling is more effective at large scale but harder to do. Width scaling beats depth scaling.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses EGNN model-size and dataset-size sweeps for atomistic materials and measures final test loss; it does not reproduce language-model pretraining-loss experiments or fit the original language-model scaling equations.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcome varies with model size, dataset size, and architecture depth versus width. The authors attribute the 0.1-to-0.2 TB loss change partly to a possible training/test distribution mismatch.

fits_no_version.finding: On 0.4 TB data with 10–100M-parameter EGNNs, widening lowers test loss, while depth beyond 3 layers raises it even as parameter count grows. The authors attribute this to over-smoothing. No fixed-parameter comparison is made.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In GNNs for atomistic modeling, how parameters are added (width vs depth) strongly changes loss, unlike transformer shape-insensitivity.

record.problems: The scaling-curve values are presented in figures without numerical values in the text; no uncertainty estimates are reported. The dataset-size sweep uses subsets of one aggregate dataset and a fixed test set from the full dataset, and the authors only conjecture a distribution mismatch for the 0.1 TB setting. No power-law fits or compute-optimal allocations are reported.

untested.parts: No language models or text pretraining loss.
No small-run fits used to predict larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation analysis. The claim that data scaling is 'more effective' at large scale is qualitative and not tied to compute.
Depth and width are not compared at fixed parameter count.
No power-law fit or exponent. No image/video, repeated-data, fine-tuning or transfer regimes. The data range is only about 1 order of magnitude.
No exponents fitted, no fitting methods compared, no published laws compared.

record.verdict_notes: The record's 'challenges' label for V5 is too strong. Loss still decreases, and the 'diminishing returns' reading comes from a semi-log plot, where a power law would also bend. The V7 'supports' label is removed: the study fits no laws and compares no fitting choices. The single-run, 10-epoch training without uncertainty estimates limits all conclusions. Section V (memory techniques) is out of scope.

versions.untested_parts: The study uses GNNs for atomistic materials modeling, not language models, and does not test held-out pretraining cross-entropy or separate parameter, token, and compute regimes.
No small-run fits are used to predict substantially larger runs.
The study does not compare parameter/token allocations at a fixed compute budget or fit compute-optimal growth trends.
Depth and width are varied, but the text does not report comparisons at fixed parameter count.
Tests scaling in atomistic-materials GNNs, but not image or video models, repeated data, fine-tuning, transfer, or other listed regimes; it does not fit a power-law form.
No downstream-task performance or relationship between downstream performance and pretraining loss is tested.
Reports curvature and a dataset-size-dependent discontinuity, but does not compare fitting methods, estimate exponents, compare published laws, or test compute-optimal splits.

rows.subject: EGNN models
rows.operation_detail: Scaled model size by increasing the number of neurons in each layer and measured final test loss.

conditions.value: same held-out test set from the 1.2 TB dataset

rows.note: The text says test loss consistently decreases across dataset sizes, but gains diminish as model size increases; it contrasts this with language- and image-model loss being nearly linear in log parameter count. Numerical curve values are not stated in the text.
rows.check: Test loss falls consistently over about 4 orders of magnitude in parameters at every data size, but with 'diminishing returns' and no power-law fit. The authors contrast this with 'nearly linear' loss vs log-params, read off a semi-log plot (Fig. 3). A pure power law also flattens on such axes, so the curve neither confirms nor refutes the power-law form. The V7 link is dropped: no exponents or fitting choices are compared.

rows.subject: EGNN models
rows.operation_detail: Scaled the training dataset by sampling increasingly large subsets of the 1.2 TB aggregate dataset and measured final test loss.

conditions.value: same held-out test set from the 1.2 TB dataset

rows.note: The text reports a noticeable loss drop from 0.1 TB to 0.2 TB and a steadier decrease beyond 0.2 TB. It conjectures the initial jump reflects a training/test distribution mismatch because the test set is drawn from the complete dataset. No power-law fit or numerical loss values are stated.
rows.check: Loss decreases with data at all model sizes (Fig. 4). Beyond 0.2 TB the authors call it 'steadily and predictably' consistent with LLM results. The 0.1 to 0.2 TB jump is conjectured to come from train/test distribution mismatch. The range is only about one order of magnitude and no fit is given. The V7 link is dropped because no fitting or setup choice is varied.

rows.subject: EGNN models
rows.operation_detail: Varied the number of neurons per layer to examine model width and measured test loss.

conditions.value: width (number of neurons in each layer)

rows.note: The text says increasing width consistently lowers test loss, but does not state numerical values or establish that the comparisons hold parameter count fixed.
rows.check: Width is varied without holding parameter count fixed, so the row does not bear on V4 as stated.

rows.subject: EGNN models
rows.operation_detail: Varied the number of layers to examine model depth and measured test loss.
rows.note: The text says increasing the number of layers beyond three raises test loss, even when total model size increases. The study does not state that depth comparisons are at fixed parameter count.
rows.check: Depth is varied without holding parameter count fixed. Loss rises beyond 3 layers even as size grows, but no fixed-parameter comparison is made.

relationships.condition: EGNN model-size scaling, 0.1M–2B params, 0.1–1.2 TB atomistic data, 10 epochs
relationships.reason: Loss decreases monotonically across 4 orders of magnitude, but with diminishing returns the authors say differ from LM/image trends. No power-law fit is given, so the form is unconfirmed (R1).
relationships.display_finding: Loss decreased monotonically across four orders of magnitude in model size, with diminishing returns that differed from language and image trends and without a fitted power law.

relationships.reason: Loss falls steadily beyond 0.2 TB, which the authors call consistent with LLMs, but the range is about one order of magnitude and has no fit. The early jump depends on data subset composition (R2).
relationships.display_finding: Loss decreased steadily beyond 0.2 TB over about one data decade, while the early jump depended on subset composition and the power-law form remained untested.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Atomistic-materials EGNN model-size scaling across the tested dataset sizes
reader_labels.reason: Test loss decreases with model size but shows diminishing returns, unlike the near-linear-in-log-parameter pattern the paper attributes to language and image models (R1).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: Loss decreases as data grows, with a pronounced 0.1-to-0.2 TB drop and a steadier trend afterward, but the study does not fit or establish a power law (R2).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Tested atomistic-materials EGNN model- and dataset-size sweeps
reader_labels.reason: The model-size curve has diminishing returns, and the dataset-size curve has a pronounced initial drop followed by a steadier decrease; these results show curvature or dependence on the tested data setting rather than establishing one fitted law (R1, R2).
